naslov: How Payton Pritchard became Boston's unlikely iso king
tekst:
PAYTON PRITCHARD IS at the Celtics bench when he feels a tap on his shoulder.
It's late April, and time is running out in Game 3 of the first round of the playoffs. Boston has padded its lead to 103-98 with just over a minute to go, and a win on the road in Philadelphia is in sight. That's what the Celtics usually do, after all: beat the Sixers in the playoffs, every time they've met in the postseason in the past 44 years. Pritchard has rained 3s tonight, five in all, to help with their latest effort, so who knows what kind of Philly-cooked hospitality awaits Pritchard right now.
He turns to find a man even shorter than he is -- a rarity for Pritchard on NBA courts -- who is swathed in all black. Black leather jacket, black T-shirt, black baseball cap. It all provides a stark canvas for the man's necklace, a blinged-out Roman numeral III, that glints when it hits the arena lights just right, and --
"Oh, s---," Pritchard thinks. "That's ..."
Allen Iverson looks at Pritchard, Pritchard remembers, and says: "You're the coldest white boy I've ever seen."
A CASE STUDY in being cold: Nobody in the league had a better effective field goal percentage on isolation plays than Pritchard last season (58.6%). Not Nikola Jokic (57.1%), nor Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (56.4%), nor Luka Doncic (55.8%). At the midpoint of the 2025-26 season, he was averaging 1.30 points per iso possession (minimum 100 possessions), according to Stat Defender, and had he kept up that pace, it would've been the highest mark for any player in the past decade. Pritchard trailed off in the second half of the season, but according to NBA.com, his 1.11 PPP for the season was still third highest in the league, placing him behind Doncic and SGA.
He is the NBA's unlikeliest iso king. And so it only makes sense that in the presence of Iverson, patron saint of undersized iso kings, Pritchard's most urgent thought is this: "That's AI."
And his second-most urgent thought: "I gotta turn up. Now I gotta go crazy."
The Celtics have been toying with the Sixers' emotions in the fourth quarter, letting them get close late -- down by three points, then one, then two. At which point, with a little more than a minute left, Pritchard decides to break some spirits.
"HE'S A KILLER," play-by-play man Eric Collins screams on the broadcast, fittingly, as Pritchard sinks a step-back 26-footer right as the buzzer sounds.
Pritchard saves most of his fireworks for Game 4, though, two days later. He nails a one-legged, buzzer-beating 3 at the end of the first quarter; carries Boston in the first half -- he scores 18 points to the starting five's combined 24; and finishes the night with a game and playoff career-high 32.
Pritchard does all this from the bench because that's what he is: a bench player. In fact, he's the gold standard for bench players, two seasons removed from being crowned Sixth Man of the Year. Actually, he's a starter in this league, or at least can be, like he was last season for 50 games, after Jrue Holiday departed for Portland and Jayson Tatum obliterated his Achilles. Then again, he's the gimmick guy (those half-court heaves) and/or the fundamentals guy (those viral handles) and/or the guy who simply rose above his station (that late first-round draft nod), who has never looked the part of NBA player. Let alone star -- or sometimes starter -- for one of the league's heavyweights.
"He's 6-1 soaking wet," says Celtics assistant coach Sam Cassell, which isn't quite right and is also, somehow, exactly right.
If this countercultural iso star is a killer, he's a trained one. For years, Pritchard has held borderline-unhinged offseason workouts that, to those close to him, bring to mind some of the biggest one-name guard icons in the history of the sport. They happen in anonymous gyms, and they're against only those who dare to meet him -- and defend him -- at his level.
The Celtics will need every bit of them. And him.
Boston leaned on Pritchard's services plenty in the before-times. Before last postseason spiraled into disaster, when the Celtics parlayed a 3-1 series lead over Philly into a nausea-inducing Game 7 loss. Before they sent Jaylen Brown packing in the offseason to -- of all places -- Philadelphia.
But now, if the Celtics hope to reclaim their spot atop an Eastern Conference that has grown only more cutthroat, they'll need Pritchard to be even colder.
"THERE'S JUST SOMETHING about a humid gym," Pritchard says.
It's 6:45 in the morning in the middle of June, and Pritchard has just walked into the humid gym of his choice, at a high school on the southeastern tip of Cape Cod. He'd pulled up to school grounds 10 minutes earlier but had to wait outside while his trainer, Michael Soares, phoned a staffer to open the locked double doors.
This gym, like most of the unglamorous gyms Pritchard handpicks for his offseason workouts, doesn't boast amenities such as air-conditioning. A few years ago, a heat wave slammed West Linn, Oregon, where he grew up. Outside, temperatures ticked up to 115 degrees, and it grew only more tropical indoors, hitting 120 in the gym at his high school alma mater, where he was conducting workouts. Pritchard came armed with extra towels because even the ball was sweating that day.
The conditions in his Cape Cod accommodations are temperate by comparison. And anyway, Pritchard likes the muck.
The muck is why he has been recruiting Division II and III basketball players, international guys and hometown buddies to high school gyms for years now. They're not exactly a ragtag motley crew, but they're not polished professionals either, and Pritchard figures that makes them hungry. He'll pay for their gas to drive down from Boston to the Cape, or their flights to cross the country or an ocean, because they can be counted on to play feisty, relentless one-on-one defense.
